A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same authors' work on multidimensional interpolation and adaptive inference paths, despite the changed title. Text, equations, tables, and figures support comparison throughout; v1 ends with references, while v2 includes readable Appendices A–C.

before.justification: V1 reports original CIFAR-10 experiments, including FID-50k comparisons, interpolation-scale sensitivity, and results from optimized inference paths in Table 1 and Figures 4–5.

after.justification: V2 reports original CIFAR-10 and ImageNet-32 experiments, model comparisons, controlled ablations, and generated examples in the main text and appendices.

M1.justification: V2 extends the proposed training construction beyond SI endpoint prediction to flow-matching velocity prediction and DDPM noise prediction with their respective objectives and inference fields. Section 4.1 also revises the low-pass construction from image-sized noise to an enlarged tensor followed by edge cropping. The SI Fourier parameterization and frozen-model adversarial path optimization remain essentially unchanged.

E1.justification: V1 evaluates only CIFAR-10. V2 adds training and evaluation on ImageNet-32, including unoptimized and adaptive-path generation. This substantially broadens the evaluated image distribution, although image generation remains the task.

E2.justification: V1's quantitative comparison uses SIbasic and SImodified as controls for SI-based variants. V2 Tables 1 and 7 add evaluated scalar-time FM and DDPM comparators, including modified-conditioning controls in Table 7. SIbasic is renamed SI, and SImodified remains in the appendix rather than being removed.

E3.justification: V2 specifies 10-NFE path optimization, whereas v1 reports adaptive-path evaluations at 10, 20, and 50 NFE. New experimental designs control kernel width, path-network input, retained output dimensions, and Fourier basis count M=10 versus M=30. Added ImageNet-32 experiments use distinct model sizes and training budgets. The retained CIFAR-10 base-training budget and FID-50k metric remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's scale sensitivity and final-image comparisons, v2 adds kernel-width sensitivity, constant/noise/x0 conditioning controls, and comparisons of training-time spatial range in Tables 2–4. Figure 6 tests path dimensionality and Fourier basis count; Appendix A adds frequency-spectrum analysis, and Figures 5 and 9 examine intermediate trajectories. These directly investigate previously untested method components.

E5.justification: V1 gives point FIDs without repetition or uncertainty information. Appendix B.3 newly states that each FID calculation is performed three times and the minimum reported, describing random variation as generally within ±2%. This is newly disclosed evaluation repetition, not evidence of increased independent training runs; seeds, confidence intervals, and result-specific dispersion remain unreported.

E6.justification: Reported CIFAR-10 scalar-SI FID at 10 NFE changes from 17.20 to 14.43; adaptive LPFI/LPFT with s=0.1 changes from 8.58 to 4.14. These are revised reported outcomes, without established equivalence of all configurations and selection rules. V2 adds extensive FM, DDPM, and ImageNet-32 results, including adaptive ImageNet-32 FID 7.06 and cases where tensor time worsens DDPM. V1's adaptive 20- and 50-NFE entries are not retained.

T1.justification: Section 3.2 adds mathematical definitions of Gaussian conditional paths, FM velocity and loss, and DDPM schedules, loss, and probability-flow inference. The low-pass definition also incorporates edge cropping. The SI transport/score theorem and normalized Fourier path construction are retained in equivalent notation; no new theorem or proof is supplied.

C1.justification: The central contributions—multidimensional training and adaptive path optimization under fixed solver configurations—remain. V2's abstract and introduction qualify training benefits as applying to some models. Its conclusion adds an approximately fifteenfold NFE-reduction claim and claims concerning the importance of x0 conditioning, path dimensionality, and training-time spatial range.

C2.justification: V1 discusses training burden and adjacent-pixel differences. V2 adds a straight-versus-curved vector-field hypothesis for SI/FM versus DDPM, connects high-frequency components to CNN locality, and interprets the new conditioning and dimensionality controls. Section 7 newly identifies limited generalizability, Euler-only testing, optimization time/VRAM costs, and dependence on the training solver configuration.

D1.justification: V2 Section 5.1 and Appendix B substantially expand v1's brief implementation description: network dimensions, path-network and discriminator architectures, kernel and noise-tensor sizes, Adam and EMA parameters, path-training budgets, warmups, and dataset-specific hardware configurations. Best-checkpoint selection using FID every 10,000 steps is newly disclosed. These disclosures do not establish that previously unspecified settings changed.

R1.justification: V2 adds DDPM/DDIM discussion and citations for those methods, FID, CIFAR-10, ImageNet/downsampled ImageNet, and U-Net. The existing positioning relative to SI, transport coupling, and prior path optimization remains substantially intact. The expanded PyTorch-FID reference identifies the same resource already cited in v1.

P1.justification: The title and terminology change throughout from multidimensional interpolants to tensor-valued time. The introduction and method exposition are extensively rewritten, preliminaries are divided into SI and flow/diffusion subsections, and results become organized discussions of individual effects. A limitations section and structured Appendices A–C substantially revise the document's narrative organization.

P2.justification: V2 adds an input-conditioning schematic and redraws the optimization schematic to expose the Fourier construction. Figure 4 uses logarithmic FID axes, and final-image comparisons become trajectory displays. The main table is reorganized across model families and datasets, with detailed controls in Appendix Table 7. New ablation tables, dimensionality plots, spectrum visualizations, and sample grids substantially expand the visual presentation.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially addresses v1's narrow empirical validation and incomplete implementation documentation. ImageNet-32 and FM/DDPM comparisons establish broader applicability boundaries, including negative DDPM findings; component ablations provide evidence for design choices previously supported mainly by intuition. Appendix B and Section 7 improve reproducibility and explain practical constraints. Minimum-FID and best-checkpoint reporting still leave uncertainty incompletely characterized, but the stronger evidence and clearer qualifications constitute a substantial overall quality improvement.
